lead: On the last day of May the Church remembers Mary’s visit to Elizabeth, and the two readings fit together closely. Paul gives the Romans a picture of genuine love: warm affection, zeal that does not lag, hospitality to strangers, joy with those who rejoice, and a heart that goes down to the lowly. In Luke, Mary lives that picture before it was written. Carrying the Son of God, she sets out with haste to serve her older kinswoman, and when she greets her, the child in Elizabeth’s womb leaps for joy. The same Greek word links the two readings: Paul’s “zeal” and Mary’s “haste” are both spoudē. Love that is real does not wait; it goes.

set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome from Corinth, about AD 57, before he had visited them. In chapters 1–11 he set out the Gospel: all have sinned, and all are justified by grace through faith in Christ. Chapter 12 turns to life. It begins, “present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (12:1), and speaks of the Church as one body with many gifts (12:4–8). Then comes a string of short, vivid commands, all describing love in practice.
str: v. 9: the heading: let love be genuine; hate evil, hold fast to good.
vv. 10–12: love among believers: affection, honour, zeal, ardour, hope, patience, prayer.
v. 13: love that gives: share with the saints in need; pursue hospitality.
vv. 14–16: love toward all: bless persecutors; rejoice and weep with others; live in harmony; associate with the lowly.
kw: Literally “without hypocrisy”, without a mask. The hypokritēs was an actor on the stage. Christian love is not a role played in church; it is the truth of the heart.
In verse 11 Paul says, “Do not lag in zeal.” Luke uses the same word when Mary goes “with haste” to Elizabeth (Luke 1:39). Christian zeal is the eagerness of love.

Literally “love of strangers”. Paul says to “pursue” it, the verb for running after something. Hospitality was essential for travelling missionaries and for the poor in the early Church (Hebrews 13:2).
vv: Let love be genuine; hate what is evil, hold fast to what is good
Love is not softness toward evil. Genuine love hates what destroys the beloved and clings to what is good for him.
Do not lag in zeal, be ardent in spirit, serve the Lord.
“Ardent” is literally “boiling”. The Spirit sets the heart on fire, and that fire shows itself in service.
Contribute to the needs of the saints; extend hospitality to strangers.
“The saints” are fellow Christians. Paul was then gathering a collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (15:25–26).
Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.
It is often easier to weep with others than to rejoice with them without envy. The Visitation is a meeting of shared joy.
do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly
The Greek can mean lowly people or lowly tasks. Both are true of Mary, who calls herself the Lord’s servant (Luke 1:38) and goes to serve.
ch: The Catechism, describing the new law of the Gospel, quotes these very verses as part of the moral teaching of the apostles: let love be genuine; hate what is evil; love one another with brotherly affection; rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer; contribute to the needs of the saints, practise hospitality (CCC 1971). It is a portrait of the Christian life lived by grace, and the Church sees it already drawn in Mary, who believed, hastened to serve, and rejoiced with her kinswoman.

set: At the Annunciation the angel told Mary that her kinswoman Elizabeth, who had been called barren, was in her sixth month (1:36). Mary, having said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord” (1:38), sets out at once for the hill country of Judea. A tradition places Zechariah’s home at Ain Karim, west of Jerusalem, several days’ walk from Nazareth.

Luke tells the scene with echoes of the Ark of the Covenant being brought up to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). David asked, “How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (2 Samuel 6:9); Elizabeth asks, “Why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?” David danced before the ark (6:14); John leaps in the womb. The ark stayed three months in the house of Obed-edom (6:11); Mary stays with Elizabeth about three months (Luke 1:56).
str: vv. 39–40: Mary sets out with haste, enters Zechariah’s house and greets Elizabeth.
v. 41: at Mary’s greeting the child leaps; Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit.
vv. 42–43: Elizabeth’s loud cry: blessed are you among women; the mother of my Lord.
v. 44: the child leaped for joy.
v. 45: blessed is she who believed.
kw: Not nervous hurry but eager readiness. St Ambrose says that the grace of the Holy Spirit knows nothing of slow efforts (in substance, Exposition of Luke 2.19).

The word the Greek Old Testament uses for Jacob and Esau struggling in Rebekah’s womb (Genesis 25:22). Here it is a leap of joy: the unborn prophet greets his Lord, as the angel had said John would be filled with the Holy Spirit even before his birth (1:15).
In Luke “the Lord” is the name of God (1:6, 9, 11), and also of Jesus (2:11). Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, confesses that the child in Mary’s womb is her Lord.
vv: In those days Mary set out and went with haste to a Judean town in the hill country
Mary does not stay at home to keep her secret. The first thing she does after receiving Christ is to carry him to someone else.
When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the child leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit
It is through Mary’s greeting that Christ’s presence reaches John and the Spirit fills Elizabeth. Mary’s voice becomes the means of grace.
Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.
The Church joins these words to the angel’s greeting in the Hail Mary. Mary is blessed because of the fruit of her womb, and the two blessings belong together.
And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?
The older woman, wife of a priest, humbles herself before the young girl from Nazareth. Faith sees the greatness that the world does not.
And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.
A different word for “blessed” (makaria), the word of the Beatitudes. Mary is happy because she believed. Zechariah had doubted (1:20); Mary trusted.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Mary, called in the Gospels “the mother of Jesus”, is acclaimed by Elizabeth, at the prompting of the Spirit, even before the birth of her son, as “the mother of my Lord”; for this reason the Church confesses that Mary is truly the Mother of God, Theotokos (CCC 495). It sees in Mary the ark of the covenant, the place where the glory of the Lord dwells (CCC 2676), and in John, filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb, the forerunner who rejoices at Christ’s coming (CCC 717). It calls Mary the most perfect embodiment of the obedience of faith, and quotes Elizabeth’s words, “Blessed is she who believed” (CCC 148).

qa: How can the Church call Mary “Mother of God” from this Gospel?

Elizabeth calls Mary “the mother of my Lord”, using the title Luke gives to God. The child in Mary’s womb is one person, the eternal Son of God, who took flesh from her. A mother is mother of a person, not only of a body, so Mary is truly the Mother of God. The Council of Ephesus (431) proclaimed this faith, and the Church professes it in every age (CCC 466, 495).
Why did Mary go “with haste”? Was she anxious?

Luke does not say she was anxious, but that she went eagerly. The angel’s word had told her of Elizabeth’s need and joy, and Mary, who had just called herself the Lord’s servant, goes to serve. The World Youth Day held in Lisbon in 2023 took this verse as its theme, and Pope Francis spoke of Mary’s haste as the readiness of love, not anxious hurry. Paul’s word to the Romans, “Do not lag in zeal”, uses the same Greek word.
rite: In Kerala the month of May is kept as the month of Mary, with daily devotions in many Syro-Malabar parishes and homes, and today that month comes to its close with the Visitation. It falls this year in the Season of the Apostles, which suits it well: Mary is the first to carry Christ to another house, before any apostle was sent.

Families can make this day a small visitation of their own: a visit to a sick relative, an elderly neighbour, a mother expecting a child. As Mary’s greeting brought joy and the Spirit into Zechariah’s house, our visits, made with prayer, can bring Christ into the homes we enter. The Hail Mary we pray at home holds Elizabeth’s very words.
study: Paul says, “Let love be genuine.” Where might my love wear a mask, and what would make it more real?
Mary went “with haste” to serve. Is there a visit or a service I keep putting off that I can make soon?
Elizabeth recognised Christ hidden in Mary before he was born. How can I learn to recognise Christ hidden in others, especially the unborn, the sick and the lowly?
“Blessed is she who believed.” What promise of the Lord am I being asked to trust, though I cannot yet see it fulfilled?
